opposingBeliefs: Renewables alone can solve climate change
Nuclear waste is an unsolvable problem
mainClaim: Nuclear energy is statistically the safest and cleanest energy source per unit of energy produced, with lower deaths and emissions than all alternatives including renewables
evidence: Kharecha and Hansen (Environmental Science & Technology, 2013) used historical production data to calculate that global nuclear power has prevented an average of 1.84 million air pollution-related deaths and 64 gigatonnes of CO2-equivalent greenhouse gas emissions that fossil fuel burning would have caused. They also project that nuclear power could prevent a further 420,000 to 7.04 million deaths and 80 to 240 GtCO2-eq by mid-century, depending on which fuel it replaces.
supportingPoints: Chernobyl (56 direct deaths) and Fukushima (1 radiation death) are outliers; modern reactors have passive safety systems
Nuclear waste volume is tiny: all US nuclear waste from 60 years fits in one football field 10 yards deep
New reactor designs (SMRs, Gen IV) are walk-away safe - shut down without human intervention
Nuclear has 90%+ capacity factor vs solar 25%, wind 35%
Lifecycle emissions including construction: nuclear 12g CO2/kWh vs solar 48g, wind 11g
France and Sweden decarbonized grids in 15 years using nuclear
limitations: The cited paper compares nuclear power with fossil fuels. It does not rank nuclear against renewables, so the 'safer than all alternatives including renewables' framing is not established by this source. High upfront capital costs ($6-9 billion per plant). Construction takes 5-10 years. Public perception remains negative. Waste requires 10,000+ year storage (though volume is small). Proliferation risks exist but are manageable. Not flexible for load following without expensive design.
counterCounterArguments: SMRs (Small Modular Reactors) reduce capital costs and construction time
Waste can be recycled in Gen IV reactors, reducing storage needs 95%
Public education can shift perception as climate urgency increases

sourceMetadata.title: Prevented Mortality and Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Historical and Projected Nuclear Power
sourceMetadata.institution: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies; Columbia University Earth Institute
sourceMetadata.methodology: Calculation from historical global energy production data; projections under scenarios
